name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q01 - Age of universe and Big Bang theory

questiontext.text: According to the Big Bang theory, approximately how old is the universe?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The origin of life on Earth is understood in the context of the origin of Earth and the universe itself.

Step 2: Evaluation
The Big Bang theory explains the origin of the universe as a singular huge explosion unimaginable in physical terms, followed by expansion and cooling. The universe is estimated to be almost 20 billion years old.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The age of the universe is approximately 20 billion years.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q02 - Formation of Earth and first appearance of life

questiontext.text: Life appeared on Earth approximately how long after the formation of Earth?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Earth formed in the solar system of the Milky Way galaxy, and life appeared only after the planet cooled sufficiently for oceans to form.

Step 2: Evaluation
Earth is supposed to have formed about 4.5 billion years ago. Life appeared 500 million years after the formation of Earth, i.e., almost 4 billion years ago.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Life appeared approximately 500 million years after Earth's formation.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q03 - Early Earth atmosphere and UV breakdown of water

questiontext.text: On early Earth, there was no atmosphere initially, and the surface was covered by gases released from molten mass. Which gas escaped into space after UV rays broke up water into hydrogen and oxygen?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Early Earth's surface was covered by water vapour, methane, carbon dioxide, and ammonia released from molten mass.

Step 2: Evaluation
Solar UV rays broke up water into hydrogen (\(H_2\)) and oxygen (\(O_2\)). Because hydrogen is lighter, \(H_2\) escaped, while oxygen combined with ammonia and methane to form water, \(CO_2\), and other compounds, eventually leading to ozone layer formation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The lighter gas that escaped was hydrogen (\(H_2\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q04 - Panspermia theory and spores from outer space

questiontext.text: The idea that units of life called 'spores' were transferred to different planets including Earth from outer space is known as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Several early hypotheses attempted to explain how life first arrived on Earth.

Step 2: Evaluation
Early Greek thinkers proposed that units of life called spores were transferred to different planets including Earth, an idea known as Panspermia, which remains a favourite hypothesis for some astronomers.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
This concept is called Panspermia.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q05 - Louis Pasteur experiment disproving spontaneous generation

questiontext.text: What did Louis Pasteur demonstrate through his experiments with killed yeast in pre-sterilised closed flasks versus flasks open to air?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For a long time, the theory of spontaneous generation claimed that life arose from decaying and rotting matter like straw and mud.

Step 2: Evaluation
Louis Pasteur showed that in pre-sterilised closed flasks, no life arose from killed yeast, whereas in flasks open to air, new living organisms appeared from airborne microbes. This proved that life comes only from pre-existing life and dismissed spontaneous generation once and for all.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Pasteur demonstrated that life comes only from pre-existing life.

answer.text: Life comes only from pre-existing life, disproving spontaneous generation
Amino acids can be synthesised from inorganic gases at \(800^\circ\text{C}\)
Life originated spontaneously from decaying organic matter
First cellular forms of life originated in terrestrial soil

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q06 - Oparin and Haldane chemical evolution hypothesis

questiontext.text: Oparin of Russia and Haldane of England proposed that the first form of life could have come from:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
While Pasteur disproved spontaneous generation under present-day conditions, Oparin and Haldane addressed how the first life form could have originated on primitive Earth.

Step 2: Evaluation
They proposed that the first form of life could have come from pre-existing non-living organic molecules (such as RNA and proteins), and that the formation of life was preceded by chemical evolution—the formation of diverse organic molecules from inorganic constituents.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Life arose from pre-existing non-living organic molecules following chemical evolution.

answer.text: Spores transferred from meteorites in outer space
Pre-existing non-living organic molecules preceded by chemical evolution
Direct conversion of decaying straw and mud into microorganisms

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q07 - Miller experiment gases temperature and products

questiontext.text: In 1953, S.L. Miller created an electric discharge in a closed flask at \(800^\circ\text{C}\) containing which set of gases, and what did he observe?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
S.L. Miller simulated early Earth's reducing atmosphere and high-energy conditions on a laboratory scale.

Step 2: Evaluation
His closed flask contained methane (\(CH_4\)), hydrogen (\(H_2\)), ammonia (\(NH_3\)), and water vapour at \(800^\circ\text{C}\). Upon passing an electric discharge, he observed the formation of amino acids.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The gas mixture was \(CH_4, H_2, NH_3,\) and water vapour, and the observed products were amino acids.

answer.text: \(CH_4, O_2, N_2\), and water vapour; formation of glucose
\(CO_2, H_2, NH_3\), and \(O_2\); formation of nucleic acids
\(CH_4, H_2, NH_3\), and water vapour; formation of amino acids
\(CH_4, CO_2, N_2\), and \(O_2\); formation of fatty acids

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q08 - Origin of non-cellular versus cellular forms of life

questiontext.text: Which statement accurately distinguishes the origin of the first non-cellular forms of life from the first cellular forms of life?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Abiogenesis proposes a gradual transition from non-living organic molecules to non-cellular giant molecules and finally to cellular life.

Step 2: Evaluation
The first non-cellular forms of life could have originated 3 billion years ago as giant molecules (RNA, protein, polysaccharides). The first cellular forms of life (probably single cells) did not originate until about 2000 million years ago, and all life forms were in a water environment only.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Non-cellular giant molecules originated about 3 billion years ago, whereas single-celled cellular forms originated about 2000 million years ago in water.

answer.text: Non-cellular forms originated 2000 million years ago on land, while cellular forms originated 3 billion years ago
Both non-cellular and cellular forms originated simultaneously 4.5 billion years ago
First cellular forms were multicellular organisms that originated 3 billion years ago
Non-cellular forms originated about 3 billion years ago as giant molecules, whereas the first cellular forms originated about 2000 million years ago in water

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q09 - Connotations of the theory of special creation

questiontext.text: Which of the following is NOT one of the three connotations of the conventional theory of special creation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Conventional religious literature describes the theory of special creation through three specific claims.

Step 2: Evaluation
The three connotations are: (1) all living organisms we see today were created as such; (2) diversity was always the same since creation and will remain the same in future; and (3) Earth is about 4000 years old. Gradual evolution from common ancestors over billions of years is Darwin's conclusion, which challenged special creation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The idea that existing life forms share common ancestors and evolved gradually over billions of years is not part of special creation.

answer.text: Existing life forms share common ancestors and evolved gradually over billions of years
All living organisms that we see today were created as such
Biodiversity was always the same since creation and will remain the same in future

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q10 - Darwin voyage on HMS Beagle and Alfred Wallace

questiontext.text: Which naturalist worked in the Malay Archipelago and independently arrived at conclusions similar to Charles Darwin's observations made aboard H.M.S. Beagle?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
During the nineteenth century, naturalists studying biodiversity across different regions converged on natural selection as the mechanism of evolution.

Step 2: Evaluation
Charles Darwin made his observations during a round-the-world voyage in the sail ship H.M.S. Beagle, while Alfred Wallace, a naturalist working in the Malay Archipelago, came to similar conclusions around the same time.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The naturalist was Alfred Wallace.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q11 - Darwinian meaning of fitness

questiontext.text: According to Charles Darwin, the term 'fitness' of an individual or population refers ultimately and only to:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In Darwinian theory, natural selection favours individuals with heritable variations that enhance survival and reproduction in a given environment.

Step 2: Evaluation
Darwin explicitly stated that fitness refers ultimately and only to reproductive fitness—individuals who are better fit in an environment leave more progeny than others, survive more, and are selected by nature.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Darwinian fitness refers ultimately and only to reproductive fitness.

answer.text: Ability to acquire new somatic traits through use and disuse

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q12 - Correlation of geological and biological history

questiontext.text: Which conclusion is supported by the observation that all existing life forms share similarities and common ancestors present at different epochs, periods, and eras?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The fossil record and comparative studies link the timeline of Earth's crust with the appearance and extinction of species.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because ancestors were present at different periods in Earth's history (epochs, periods, and eras), the geological history of Earth closely correlates with its biological history, leading to the conclusion that Earth is billions of years old rather than a few thousand years old.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The geological history of Earth closely correlates with its biological history, and Earth is billions of years old.

answer.text: No extinctions occurred before the appearance of mammals
All ancestral species originated simultaneously in the same era
The geological history of Earth closely correlates with its biological history, and Earth is billions of years old

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q13 - Natural selection as mechanism of evolution

questiontext.text: In Darwinian theory, what is the mechanism by which better-adapted individuals survive more and leave more progeny?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Populations possess built-in variations in characteristics that affect survival under natural conditions.

Step 2: Evaluation
Those better fit in an environment outbreed others, survive more, and are selected by nature. Darwin called this process natural selection and implied it as a mechanism of evolution.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The mechanism is natural selection.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q14 - Paleontological evidence from sedimentary rock layers

questiontext.text: The study of fossils found in different-aged sedimentary rock layers, which shows that certain life forms are restricted to specific geological time-spans, is called:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Fossils are the remains of hard parts of life forms preserved in sedimentary rocks.

Step 2: Evaluation
Examining fossils across different sedimentary layers indicates the geological periods in which those organisms existed, showing that new forms of life arose at different times in Earth's history. This constitutes paleontological evidence.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
This is called paleontological evidence.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q15 - Embryological support Haeckel versus von Baer

questiontext.text: Ernst Haeckel's proposal of embryological support for evolution, based on features like vestigial gill slits in vertebrate embryos, was disapproved by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ernst Haeckel observed that all vertebrate embryos, including humans, develop a row of vestigial gill slits behind the head, which are functional only in adult fish.

Step 2: Evaluation
However, careful study performed by Karl Ernst von Baer disapproved this proposal, as he noted that embryos never pass through the adult stages of other animals.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Haeckel's proposal was disapproved by Karl Ernst von Baer.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q16 - Homologous forelimbs in mammals and divergent evolution

questiontext.text: Whales, bats, cheetahs, and humans share the same basic pattern of forelimb bones (humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, and phalanges) despite performing different functions. This is an example of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Comparative anatomy reveals whether diverse organisms share common ancestors.

Step 2: Evaluation
In whales, bats, cheetahs, and humans, the same anatomical forelimb structure developed along different directions due to adaptations to different needs. Such structures are homologous and result from divergent evolution, indicating common ancestry.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
This exemplifies divergent evolution and homologous structures.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q17 - Homology in plants Bougainvillea and Cucurbita

questiontext.text: Which pair of plant structures represents homology based on divergent evolution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Homologous structures in plants share a common anatomical origin (such as axillary buds) while performing different functions.

Step 2: Evaluation
The thorn of Bougainvillea and the tendril of Cucurbita are both stem modifications arising from axillary buds, representing homology. By contrast, sweet potato (root modification) and potato (stem modification) represent analogy.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The thorn of Bougainvillea and tendril of Cucurbita represent homology.

answer.text: Wings of butterfly and wings of birds
Flippers of penguins and flippers of dolphins

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q18 - Analogous structures and convergent evolution

questiontext.text: The eye of the octopus and the eye of mammals, as well as the flippers of penguins and dolphins, are examples of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
When organisms from different lineages occupy similar habitats, they often evolve anatomically different structures to perform the same function.

Step 2: Evaluation
The eye of the octopus and of mammals, and the flippers of penguins and dolphins, are not anatomically similar structures though they perform similar functions. Hence, they are analogous structures resulting from convergent evolution.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
They are analogous structures resulting from convergent evolution.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q19 - Sweet potato and potato as plant analogy

questiontext.text: Sweet potato and potato are considered analogous structures because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Analogy refers to different structures evolving for the same function and thus showing superficial similarity.

Step 2: Evaluation
Sweet potato is a root modification, whereas potato is a stem modification. Despite having different anatomical origins, both are modified for the same function of food storage.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
They have different anatomical origins (root versus stem) but perform the same function.

answer.text: Both are stem modifications performing different functions
Both are root modifications indicating common ancestry
Sweet potato is a root modification and potato is a stem modification, yet both perform the same function
Sweet potato is a stem modification and potato is a root modification, representing divergent evolution

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q20 - Biochemical similarities in proteins and genes

questiontext.text: Similarities in proteins and genes performing a given function among diverse organisms provide evidence for:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Evolutionary relationships can be inferred not only from comparative anatomy but also from molecular and biochemical comparisons.

Step 2: Evaluation
Similarities in proteins and genes performing a given function among diverse organisms point to the same shared ancestry as structural similarities (homology).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
These biochemical similarities point to common ancestry.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q21 - Artificial breeding of dogs and crops

questiontext.text: Intensive breeding programmes by humans have created distinct breeds of dogs within hundreds of years. This observation is used to argue that:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Domestication and selective breeding demonstrate how selection can rapidly produce diverse breeds from a common group.

Step 2: Evaluation
If humans can create new breeds within hundreds of years through intensive breeding, nature could certainly have produced diverse species over millions of years through natural selection.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Nature could have created diverse species over millions of years in a similar manner.

answer.text: Nature could have created new species in a similar way over millions of years
New species can only arise through human intervention
Different dog breeds belong to different biological kingdoms

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q22 - Industrial melanism lichens and moth survival

questiontext.text: In the study of industrial melanism in England (1850s vs 1920), which statement is correct regarding lichens and moth populations?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Predators spot moths against a contrasting background, and lichens serve as industrial pollution indicators because they do not grow in polluted areas.

Step 2: Evaluation
Before industrialisation, thick white-coloured lichens covered trees, favouring white-winged moths. After industrialisation, smoke and soot darkened tree trunks and lichens disappeared, favouring dark-winged (melanised) moths. In rural unpolluted areas, melanic moth counts remained low. Importantly, in a mixed population, no variant is completely wiped out.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Lichens act as pollution indicators by failing to grow in polluted areas, and neither moth variant was completely wiped out.

answer.text: White-winged moths were completely wiped out from England after 1920
Lichens act as industrial pollution indicators because they do not grow in polluted areas, and no moth variant is completely wiped out
Thick growth of white-coloured lichens increased after industrialisation in 1920
Dark-winged moths outnumbered white-winged moths in rural areas where industrialisation did not occur

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q23 - Evolution by anthropogenic action herbicides and antibiotics

questiontext.text: The rapid appearance of herbicide-resistant weeds and antibiotic-resistant microbes within months or years is an example of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Human activities can act as strong selective agents on populations with pre-existing variations.

Step 2: Evaluation
Excess use of herbicides, pesticides, and antibiotics selects for resistant varieties on a much shorter time scale of months or years rather than centuries. These are examples of evolution by anthropogenic action.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
This represents evolution by anthropogenic action.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q24 - Evolution as a stochastic process

questiontext.text: What does the emergence of resistant organisms due to anthropogenic action indicate about the nature of the evolutionary process?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Evolution does not follow a predetermined path toward a fixed goal.

Step 2: Evaluation
Examples of evolution by anthropogenic action demonstrate that evolution is not a directed process in the sense of determinism; rather, it is a stochastic process based on chance events in nature and chance mutations in organisms.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Evolution is a stochastic process based on chance events in nature and chance mutations in organisms.

answer.text: Evolution is a strictly deterministic process moving toward a fixed goal
Evolution occurs only when organisms consciously decide to adapt
Evolution always requires millions of years regardless of generation time
Evolution is a stochastic process based on chance events in nature and chance mutations

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q25 - Darwins finches in Galapagos Islands

questiontext.text: On the Galapagos Islands, Darwin's finches evolved from an original seed-eating ancestral stock into insectivorous and vegetarian finches with altered beaks. This is a classic example of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
When a single ancestral species diversifies into multiple species adapted to different habitats or diets within a geographical area, it illustrates adaptive radiation.

Step 2: Evaluation
Darwin conjectured that all varieties of finches on the Galapagos Islands evolved on the island itself from original seed-eating features into forms with altered beaks (insectivorous and vegetarian), representing adaptive radiation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Darwin's finches represent adaptive radiation.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q26 - Adaptive radiation of Australian marsupials

questiontext.text: The process of evolution of different species in a given geographical area starting from a point and literally radiating to other habitats, as seen in Australian marsupials, is called:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Geographical isolation often allows an ancestral stock to diversify into multiple ecological niches.

Step 2: Evaluation
Australian marsupials—such as the kangaroo, koala, wombat, bandicoot, and Tasmanian wolf—evolved from a single ancestral stock within the Australian island continent. This process of radiating from a point to other habitats in a given geographical area is adaptive radiation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
This phenomenon is called adaptive radiation.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q27 - Multiple adaptive radiations and convergent evolution

questiontext.text: When more than one adaptive radiation appears to have occurred in an isolated geographical area representing different habitats (such as placental mammals and marsupials in Australia), the phenomenon is called:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Two independent evolutionary radiations in the same isolated region face similar environmental pressures across comparable habitats.

Step 2: Evaluation
In Australia, both marsupials and placental mammals underwent adaptive radiation, producing pairs of organisms (e.g., placental wolf and Tasmanian wolf) that appear similar despite separate ancestries. When more than one adaptive radiation occurs in an isolated geographical area, it is called convergent evolution.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
This is called convergent evolution.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q28 - Placental mammal and Australian marsupial pair

questiontext.text: Which of the following pairs of placental mammal and Australian marsupial represents an INCORRECT match of convergent evolution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Australian marsupials and placental mammals show parallel pairs of similarly adapted forms.

Step 2: Evaluation
The correct pairs are: Mole – Marsupial mole; Anteater – Numbat; Mouse – Marsupial mouse; Lemur – Spotted cuscus; Flying squirrel – Flying phalanger; Bobcat – Tasmanian tiger cat; Wolf – Tasmanian wolf. Pairing Lemur with Numbat is incorrect because Lemur corresponds to Spotted cuscus while Anteater corresponds to Numbat.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Lemur and Numbat is the incorrect match.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q29 - Rate of appearance of new forms and life span

questiontext.text: When a bacterial colony growing on a medium experiences a change in medium composition, a variant population outgrows the others within days, whereas a similar evolutionary shift in fish or fowl takes millions of years. This difference is primarily because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The rate of appearance of new forms by natural selection is linked to the life cycle or life span of the organism.

Step 2: Evaluation
Microbes divide fast and multiply into millions of individuals within hours, allowing variant populations to outgrow others within days. In contrast, fish and fowl have life spans measured in years, so the same evolutionary process takes millions of years.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The rate of appearance of new forms is linked to the organism's life cycle or life span.

answer.text: The rate of appearance of new forms is linked to the life cycle or life span of the organism
Bacteria do not possess a genetic basis for adaptive ability
Fish and fowl are not subject to natural selection
Bacterial variants arise by Lamarckian inheritance of acquired characters

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q30 - Two key concepts of Darwinian theory

questiontext.text: What are the two key concepts of Darwinian Theory of Evolution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Darwin's theory explains both the pattern of shared ancestry among living forms and the mechanism driving adaptation.

Step 2: Evaluation
Branching descent (all organisms share common ancestors at different geological times) and natural selection (differential reproductive success of heritable variations) are the two key concepts of Darwinian Theory of Evolution.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The two key concepts are branching descent and natural selection.

answer.text: Use and disuse of organs and saltation

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q31 - Lamarck theory of use and disuse of organs

questiontext.text: Which French naturalist proposed that evolution was driven by the use and disuse of organs, using the elongation of giraffe necks as an example?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Before Darwin, an alternative hypothesis attempted to explain how organisms adapt to their environment.

Step 2: Evaluation
French naturalist Lamarck proposed that evolution of life forms occurred driven by use and disuse of organs, suggesting that giraffes elongated their necks to forage leaves on tall trees and passed this acquired character to succeeding generations.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
This theory was proposed by Lamarck.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q32 - Influence of Thomas Malthus on Darwin

questiontext.text: How did Thomas Malthus's work on populations influence Charles Darwin's concept of natural selection?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Natural selection rests on factual observations about population growth and resource availability.

Step 2: Evaluation
Theoretically, population size grows exponentially if every individual reproduces maximally, yet in reality population sizes remain limited (except for seasonal fluctuations) because natural resources are limited. This implies competition for resources, where only those with heritable variations enabling better resource utilisation survive and leave more progeny.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Limited natural resources versus potential exponential growth leads to competition, allowing better-adapted individuals to survive and reproduce.

answer.text: It showed that populations never vary in heritable characteristics
It proved that natural resources are unlimited in every habitat
It demonstrated that single-step large mutations cause instant speciation
It highlighted that potential exponential population growth against limited resources results in competition

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q33 - Hugo de Vries mutations versus Darwinian variations

questiontext.text: How do mutations described by Hugo de Vries differ from Darwinian variations?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the first decade of the twentieth century, Hugo de Vries studied evening primrose and proposed mutation as the cause of evolution.

Step 2: Evaluation
Mutations are large differences arising suddenly in a population, and they are random and directionless, causing speciation via saltation (single-step large mutation). In contrast, Darwinian variations are small and directional, leading to gradual evolution.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Mutations are random, directionless, and cause saltation, whereas Darwinian variations are small, directional, and gradual.

answer.text: Mutations are random and directionless causing saltation, whereas Darwinian variations are small and directional
Mutations are small and directional, whereas Darwinian variations are random and directionless
Mutations always cause gradual evolution, whereas Darwinian variations cause single-step speciation
Mutations are non-heritable, whereas Darwinian variations are acquired characters

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q34 - Hardy-Weinberg calculation of heterozygote frequency

questiontext.text: In a diploid population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of homozygous recessive individuals (\(aa\)) is \(0.09\). What is the frequency of heterozygous individuals (\(Aa\)) in this population?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for a gene with two alleles \(A\) and \(a\). The frequency of homozygous recessive individuals (\(aa\)) is given as \(q^2 = 0.09\).

Step 2: Assumptions
Under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, random mating and absence of evolutionary disturbances ensure that genotype frequencies follow the binomial expansion of \((p + q)^2\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\(p + q = 1\) and \(p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1\), where \(p\) is the frequency of allele \(A\), \(q\) is the frequency of allele \(a\), and \(2pq\) is the frequency of heterozygotes (\(Aa\)).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Calculate \(q\) from \(q^2 = 0.09\):
\(q = \sqrt{0.09} = 0.3\).
2. Calculate \(p\) using \(p + q = 1\):
\(p = 1 - 0.3 = 0.7\).
3. Calculate the heterozygote frequency \(2pq\):
\(2pq = 2 \times 0.7 \times 0.3 = 0.42\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking the sum: \(p^2 = (0.7)^2 = 0.49\), \(2pq = 0.42\), \(q^2 = 0.09\); \(0.49 + 0.42 + 0.09 = 1.00\). The frequency of heterozygous individuals (\(Aa\)) is \(0.42\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q35 - Hardy-Weinberg allele frequency from genotype counts

questiontext.text: In a population of \(1000\) diploid individuals in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, \(360\) belong to genotype \(AA\), \(480\) to \(Aa\), and \(160\) to \(aa\). What is the frequency of allele \(A\) in this population?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Total population size \(N = 1000\). Genotype counts: \(AA = 360\), \(Aa = 480\), \(aa = 160\).

Step 2: Assumptions
The population is diploid and at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, so the frequency of \(AA\) is \(p^2\), \(Aa\) is \(2pq\), and \(aa\) is \(q^2\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\(p^2 = \frac{\text{Number of } AA}{N}\), and \(p + q = 1\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\(p^2 = \frac{360}{1000} = 0.36\).
Taking the square root gives:
\(p = \sqrt{0.36} = 0.6\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking with \(q^2 = \frac{160}{1000} = 0.16 \implies q = 0.4\), and \(p + q = 0.6 + 0.4 = 1.0\), with \(2pq = 2(0.6)(0.4) = 0.48\) (\(480\) individuals). Thus, the frequency of allele \(A\) is \(0.6\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q36 - Factors affecting Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium

questiontext.text: Which of the following is NOT one of the five factors known to affect Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium is maintained only when no evolutionary forces act on the gene pool.

Step 2: Evaluation
The five factors known to affect Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium are: gene migration (or gene flow), genetic drift, mutation, genetic recombination, and natural selection. Random mating in a large population maintains genetic equilibrium rather than disturbing it.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Random mating in a large population does not disturb Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q37 - Genetic drift and founder effect

questiontext.text: When a change in allele frequency occurs by chance and is so pronounced in a newly isolated sample of a population that they become a different species, the original drifted population becomes founders and the phenomenon is called:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Genetic drift refers to random fluctuations in allele frequencies occurring by chance.

Step 2: Evaluation
Sometimes, the change in allele frequency in a new drifted sample of a population is so different that the sample becomes a distinct species. The original drifted population becomes founders, and this effect is called the founder effect.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
This phenomenon is called the founder effect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q38 - Disruptive natural selection on peripheral traits

questiontext.text: Which type of natural selection occurs when more individuals acquire peripheral character values at both ends of the phenotypic distribution curve, resulting in two peaks?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Natural selection can produce three distinct patterns on a phenotypic distribution curve: stabilisation, directional change, or disruption.

Step 2: Evaluation
When more individuals acquire peripheral character values at both ends of the distribution curve, two peaks form. This is called disruptive selection (as opposed to stabilising selection favouring the mean, and directional selection shifting the peak in one direction).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
This mode of natural selection is disruptive selection.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q39 - Interpretation of disturbance in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium

questiontext.text: If the measured allele frequencies in a population differ from the values expected under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, what does this difference indicate?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium serves as a baseline where the gene pool remains constant across generations.

Step 2: Evaluation
When measured allele frequencies differ from expected values, the difference and its direction indicate the extent of evolutionary change. Disturbance in genetic equilibrium is interpreted as resulting in evolution.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The difference indicates the extent of evolutionary change occurring in the population.

answer.text: The gene pool has remained completely constant across generations
No evolutionary forces are acting on the population
Disturbance in genetic equilibrium, indicating the extent of evolutionary change
The population has achieved permanent reproductive isolation from all other species

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q40 - First organisms on land and Coelacanth lobefins

questiontext.text: Which organisms were the first to invade land, and which group of fishes with stout, strong fins (including Coelacanth caught in South Africa in 1938) evolved into the first amphibians?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The colonisation of terrestrial habitats occurred sequentially, with autotrophs establishing on land before animals.

Step 2: Evaluation
Plants were the first organisms to invade land and were widespread when animals invaded land. About 350 mya, fishes with stout and strong fins called lobefins (represented by Coelacanth, caught in South Africa in 1938 when thought extinct) could move on land and go back to water, evolving into the first amphibians.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Plants invaded land first, and lobefins evolved into the first amphibians.

answer.text: Invertebrates invaded land first; jawless fish evolved into amphibians
Amphibians invaded land first; reptiles evolved into lobefins
Jawless fish invaded land first; sea weeds evolved into plants
Plants invaded land first; lobefins evolved into the first amphibians

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q41 - Thick-shelled eggs in reptiles and Ichthyosaurus

questiontext.text: What key reproductive adaptation allowed reptiles to dominate land after evolving from amphibians, unlike amphibians whose eggs require water?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Transitioning to fully terrestrial life required reproductive independence from aquatic habitats.

Step 2: Evaluation
Amphibians evolved into reptiles, which lay thick-shelled eggs that do not dry up in the sun, unlike amphibian eggs. Modern descendants of early reptiles include turtles, tortoises, and crocodiles.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Reptiles lay thick-shelled eggs that do not dry up in the sun.

answer.text: They lay thick-shelled eggs that do not dry up in the sun
They are viviparous and protect unborn young inside the mother's body
They possess stout, strong fins for returning to water
They reproduce only in deep marine environments

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q42 - Dinosaurs extinction Tyrannosaurus rex and coal deposits

questiontext.text: Which statement about the age of reptiles and pteridophytes is accurate?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
During the dominance of reptiles, giant pteridophytes also flourished and later contributed to fossil fuel formation before the sudden extinction of dinosaurs.

Step 2: Evaluation
Giant ferns (pteridophytes) fell slowly to form coal deposits. Among land reptiles, the biggest dinosaur, Tyrannosaurus rex, was about 20 feet in height with huge dagger-like teeth. About 65 million years ago (mya), dinosaurs suddenly disappeared from Earth.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Dinosaurs suddenly disappeared about 65 mya, and giant ferns fell to form coal deposits.

answer.text: Dinosaurs disappeared about 200 mya, while Ichthyosaurus appeared 65 mya
Dinosaurs suddenly disappeared about 65 mya, and giant ferns (pteridophytes) fell to form coal deposits
Tyrannosaurus rex was a small shrew-like reptile about 2 feet in height
All reptiles of the dinosaur era became extinct, leaving no small-sized reptiles today

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q43 - Early mammals continental drift and aquatic mammals

questiontext.text: Which of the following is NOT true regarding the evolution of mammals?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Mammals took over Earth when reptiles declined, with their distribution and survival shaped by viviparity, intelligence, and continental drift.

Step 2: Evaluation
The first mammals were small and shrew-like, viviparous, and better at sensing and avoiding danger. Whales, dolphins, seals, and sea cows are mammals living wholly in water. Due to continental drift, when South America joined North America, South American mammals were overridden by North American fauna—NOT the reverse.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The false statement is that South American fauna overrode North American mammals.

answer.text: The first mammals were like shrews with small-sized fossils
Whales, dolphins, seals, and sea cows are mammals that live wholly in water
When South America joined North America, South American mammals overrode North American fauna
Australian pouched mammals survived due to lack of competition from other mammals

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q44 - Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus 15 mya

questiontext.text: About 15 million years ago, two primates existed that were hairy and walked like gorillas and chimpanzees. Which one was more man-like and which one was more ape-like?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Early Miocene primates around 15 mya represent key ancestors in the divergence of apes and hominids.

Step 2: Evaluation
About 15 mya, Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus existed; both were hairy and walked like gorillas and chimpanzees. Ramapithecus was more man-like, while Dryopithecus was more ape-like.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Ramapithecus was more man-like and Dryopithecus was more ape-like.

answer.text: Dryopithecus was more man-like; Ramapithecus was more ape-like
Australopithecus was more man-like; Homo habilis was more ape-like
Both Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus were strictly bipedal and hairless
Ramapithecus was more man-like; Dryopithecus was more ape-like

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q45 - Australopithecines habitat weapons and diet

questiontext.text: Which hominids probably lived in East African grasslands about 2 million years ago, hunted with stone weapons, and essentially ate fruit?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Early bipedal hominids in Africa transitioned from forest habitats to grasslands and began using simple stone tools.

Step 2: Evaluation
Two million years ago, Australopithecines probably lived in East African grasslands. Evidence shows they hunted with stone weapons but essentially ate fruit.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
These hominids were Australopithecines.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q46 - Homo habilis versus Homo erectus brain capacity

questiontext.text: Which pair of hominid species and brain capacities is correctly matched?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Human evolution is marked by a steady increase in cranial capacity across successive species of Homo.

Step 2: Evaluation
Homo habilis (the first human-like hominid) had a brain capacity between 650–800 cc and probably did not eat meat. Homo erectus (Java fossils, 1.5 mya) had a brain capacity around 900 cc and probably ate meat. Neanderthal man had a brain size of 1400 cc.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Homo habilis (650–800 cc) and Homo erectus (around 900 cc) is the correct match.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q47 - Neanderthal man and modern Homo sapiens

questiontext.text: Which of the following features is characteristic of Neanderthal man (1,00,000–40,000 years ago)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Neanderthal man represents a late Pleistocene hominid population with advanced behavioural traits.

Step 2: Evaluation
Neanderthal man had a brain size of 1400 cc, lived in the Near East and Central Asia between 1,00,000–40,000 years back, used hides to protect their body, and buried their dead.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Neanderthal man had a 1400 cc brain, used hides for body protection, and buried their dead.

answer.text: Brain size of 650–800 cc and lived exclusively in Java
Arose during the ice age between 75,000–10,000 years ago and started agriculture
Brain size of 1400 cc, used hides to protect their body, and buried their dead
Walked like gorillas about 15 mya and was more ape-like

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MCQ_Q48 - Pre-historic cave art Bhimbetka and agriculture

questiontext.text: Pre-historic cave art (such as the paintings at Bhimbetka rock shelter in Madhya Pradesh) and agriculture developed approximately how many years ago, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Modern Homo sapiens arose during the ice age (75,000–10,000 years ago) and subsequently developed symbolic art and settled agriculture.

Step 2: Evaluation
Pre-historic cave art developed about 18,000 years ago (seen at Bhimbetka rock shelter in Raisen district of Madhya Pradesh), and agriculture came around 10,000 years back when human settlements started.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Cave art developed about 18,000 years ago and agriculture around 10,000 years ago.
